For nearly 70 years, the Fermi Paradox has puzzled us, questioning why, given the possibility of numerous advanced civilizations, we haven't detected any evidence of them. One potential explanation is the Dyson Sphere, a hypothetical megastructure where a megastructure surrounds a star to collect vast amounts of energy for an advanced civilization. To investigate the feasibility of detecting these structures, we created the Dyson Sphere Telescope, an astronomical tool designed to search for their telltale signs in the form of unexpected extra-solar point sources of energy. This search tool can be operated with existing astronomical databases and is accessible to both professional researchers and amateur astronomers through its user-friendly interface and API. Additionally, we used k-means clustering to analyze the existing catalog of anomalous sources in our solar neighborhood, in search of any potential clues of a Dyson Sphere. Our comprehensive code is freely available to the public through GitHub.

Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this involves deploying active measurement tools, which send test traffic and gauge performance. Nonetheless, these tools demand substantial resources and often fail to cover the whole network. Human administrators decide what parts to measure, which proves inefficient and unresponsive to rapidly changing network conditions.

This research explores the potential of peer-to-peer (P2P) applications to enhance the process of measuring network performance. A P2P approach lets users share measurement resources, which could enable comprehensive network assessments. P2P applications also leverage existing traffic, avoiding the need for extra resources. We outline the advantages, challenges, and possible solutions to implementing this approach, with a focus on the specific requirements for checking service-level agreements. Our findings suggest that existing P2P applications can be adapted to carry out active measurements, but not necessarily for assessing service-level agreements. Nonetheless, most can offer a foundation for such assessments.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper extends those studies by considering feedback effects from the radiofrequency system on the beam itself. Using state space trace models, calculations demonstrate how resonant interactions between the beam and RF system can lead to an increase in the threshold beam current by up to a factor of 10 or more, mainly influenced by issues of stability in the feedback loop.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing the ultimate decay products of neutrino interactions, causing the primary detected particles to be those resulting from deep inelastic scattering with the highest energies. The implementation of multi-layered detectors, containing three-dimensional scintillator tracking sensors, opens up the possibility of constructing next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments capable of detecting all final particles with the highest energies. The incorporation of such comprehensive detector components allows the theoretical neutrino interaction models to be validated and refined with significantly greater precision. In order to take advantage of this level of detection capability, next-generation experiments will need to employ next-generation simulations that are capable of modeling both the production and detection processes with six-dimensional neutrino beams. Although simulations using such beams have been utilized in existing experiments, they have not been utilized in experiments with five-dimensional neutrino beams until now. The objective in developing such simulations, incorporating detector components as well, is to provide a foundational framework that can be utilized in the carefully crafted analysis of the future experiments.

In a previous study, we investigated the sticking forces between particles with a layer of surface water, occurring in a warm, dry, and dust-filled room in chondritic grains that may mimic the cooler conditions near the solar nebula's outer edge. Our findings revealed that the sticking forces between these grains were significantly higher than those of dry particles in that same region, but lower than those in the cooler areas near the solar nebula's outer edge. Moreover, we found that the presence of water led to a greater than 10-fold increase in grain sticking in the warm, dry regions, particularly as the temperature dropped from 280 to 200 K, aligning with observations of the solar system's outer edge's rapid accumulation of mass. To explain this phenomenon, we identified two mechanisms by which water on the grains increases their sticking rates, including the formation of a liquid bridge and the sublimation of the grains into the surrounding gas. As the solar system was accumulating its outer edge, the mass of these mass was further accelerated by the accumulation of mass. Moreover, these results indicate that the accumulation of mass was self-regulating, allowing the outer edge of the system to maintain a delicate equilibrium as it grew, which could be a key factor in explaining the location of the solar system's outer edge.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to complex unstructured scenarios. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet linear and nonlinear equality constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art methods in movement primitives and demonstrates the efficacy of EKMP through comprehensive experiments on a Uranus robotic arm, showcasing successful adaptation and constraint satisfaction in a complex real-world scenario.

To complete the one-loop central emission vertex for two gluons in the BFKL equation, we derived the central CEW for two gluons in a general kinematic setting, focusing on hard processes with three hard scales.  We derived the CEV in the general $N$-reggeon configuration, using the hard process of Hard Diffraction as a specific example, and found that in the limit of collinear singularity, the CEV simplifies to a universal form that matches the known impact factors.  We also identified a previous error in the literature related to the CEV in the $N$-reggeon configuration.  We then applied the derived CEV to the hard process of Hard Diffraction, performing numerical evaluations of the one-loop BFKL amplitude for the process of proton-proton elastic diffraction at the LHC.  We found that the color structure of the BFKL pomeron exchanged in hard diffractive processes is mainly determined by the impact factors, with the CEV having a minimal effect.  The total BFKL amplitude in the $P_q$ channel constitutes the dominant contribution to the hard diffractive process, while the BFKL amplitude in the $P_g$ channel, long considered negligible, may have a visible contribution.  We proposed that the ratio of the cross sections of hard diffractive processes with and without the BFKL pomeron in the $P_g$ channel could provide experimental proof of the magnitude

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with d-wave symmetry. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling promotes d-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair suppression. Notably, when Rashba coupling is dominant, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics in a non-equilibrium phase diagram. Furthermore, we observe that Rashba coupling induces a transition between distinct d-wave superconducting orders, with implications for the realization of topologically non-trivial superconductivity. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this approach aligns with bulk-boundary correspondence, showing that a topologically non-trivial d-wave superconducting phase is accompanied by an edge superconducting state.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point (T_c), can be identified by changes in the sound wave absorption at specific frequencies, particularly at high $x$ values, for example, $x$ = 0.28. The findings suggest that this transition represents the rotation of the interlocked vortex lattice structure by 90 degrees. Notably, the transition boundary follows the $B^{1/2}$ pattern as defined by the Ginzburg parameter, and the amplitude of the absorption, when normalized to its value in lower magnetic fields, increases with higher $x$ values, demonstrating a clear interdependence on the material's composition.

Theories describing weakly interacting polymer brushes have been expanded upon a curve. A recent concept, introducing boundary restrictions to a planar model, is now applied to curved surfaces. This extension introduces an 'end exclusion length' ($\lambda$) into the analysis, which is incorporated into the ground state energy calculation. A new, $\lambda$-dependent scaling theory is developed and a modified mean-field model is employed to verify it. It is found that the mean-field approach yields an accurate representation of the ground state density when $\lambda$ is much smaller than the Kuhn length, but exhibits overestimated energy as $\lambda$ approaches the brush height. A new, $\lambda$-inclusive scaling variant is also developed to capture high-$\lambda$ behavior, which becomes normal-height brushes at the transition point. This high-$\lambda$ regime is characterized by significant surface curvature and can be represented by rings with very long contour lengths. Notably, the theory is applicable across the entire range of $\lambda$, from short to extended brushes, without end exclusion modifications.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary matching and U-net deep learning image restoration techniques on just two weeks' worth of data. The machine learning-based method yielded significantly clearer images than the default method provided by the Fermi collaboration. Notably, it also offered more accurate $\gamma$-ray spectra for 814 identified sources, by leveraging morphological information from all-sky maps in comparison to the catalog from the 3FGL release.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a simple majority rule. Theoretical proof shows that when participants select items from a set defined by a-constrained optimization rules, a approximation of the optimal solution can be achieved. Furthermore, we identify the success function of the resulting solution as being related to a related online algorithm, and we propose a approximation of the optimal solution based on a non-preemptive algorithm.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids larger than 
40 kilometers in diameter. As existing records for wide (larger than 10 
kilometers) binary asteroids are well documented, even the smallest detected 
binaries in our study maintain a stable orbit. Notably, we found 14 new wide 
binary asteroids, including some with particularly large and rare binary 
separations. Furthermore, our data revealed a distinct distribution of log 
binary separation values, which vary depending on the aperture used for 
analysis. Due to the robustness, efficiency, and scalability of our methods, 
they can be applied to large scale surveys to identify additional wide binary 
asteroids. With this in mind, we anticipate that continuing searches using 
existing archival images will yield even more binary discoveries in the 
coming years.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third discussion expands on the results, with implications for the choice of models.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup, before applying an optimized detection algorithm and presenting a simulated performance assessment.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,
such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user
interactivity. Additionally, the adoption of modern web frameworks facilitates
extensive customization, making our visualization tools effortlessly integratable
into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is
also compatible with Aladin Lite and other popular third-party web tools.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that the Wolfcampian-Wilcoxian (Early and Middle Cretaceous) period saw the development of a Central Gondwanan rift system, with a final stage of extension affecting both Africa and South America.  This work reevaluates the timing of the Wolfcampian-Brazilian margin conjugacy and presents a model of the resulting break-up and associated sedimentation patterns.  With varying rates of extension across South Atlantic margins, researchers found that the conjugate West African and Brazilian margins stretched at rates of 10-14 and 8-10 cm/myr respectively, during the Turonian through Danian stages of the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods.  This analysis builds on the findings of Strachan et al. (2017) and incorporates updated data (Strachach et al., 2019).

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context.

Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological and geometric principles, is developed to evaluate the similarities and differences among knotted proteins, with the aim of identifying potential correlations between a protein's spatial structure and its folding behavior. This research analyzes numerous simulations and experimental data from 19 trefoil-like knotted proteins, using specific scoring measures to rank the similarities among their topological and geometric structures. Cluster analyses and further results suggest that hydrophobic interactions play a pivotal role in shaping the topological and geometric similarities of knotted proteins.

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects. These results indicate the need for additional data to refine EDE parameters and show that the impact of EDE on the acoustic scale can be distinguished from other solutions to the Hubble tension, such as neutrless massive particles and a varying effective number of neutrino species.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures. The structures in question include Heisenberg algebras, which serve as the algebraic framework, while the geometric structures comprise convex manifolds that represent the possible states. It has been demonstrated how the anomalous NG theorem can be viewed as an extension of the standard NG theorem within the context of these algebraic and geometric structures, although it has been established that the relationship is not entirely direct. The authors have further explored specific properties such as the role of central charges and the behavior of states with zero momentum in relation to the variance of operators and their connection to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and the breaking of continuous symmetries. A significant outcome has been the confirmation that the relationship between the central charges and operator variance holds for both bosonic and fermionic systems. The authors have further established that the state with the lowest possible energy forms a coherent state with respect to the algebra of NG bosons and that these bosons exhibit a non-zero vacuum expectation value. The discussion has been framed within the context of relativistic systems and the system-hamiltonian approach has been adopted to facilitate this understanding.

To address the challenge of acquiring substantial labeled datasets for complex classification tasks, Counterfactual Data Augmentation is gaining significance. It involves creating realistic altered versions of data, allowing for the expansion of available samples by referring to existing labels. While techniques like WGAN have shown success in generating counterfactual data, there's a limitation in their flexibility to adjust the desired class distribution in generated data. We introduce a new framework, DISCO, which improves counterfactual data generation by allowing adjustments to class probabilities in both source and target data, leading to enhanced flexibility. We demonstrate that DISCO-generated data is flexible and, when used for training, allows models to perform better than those trained on original datasets. Additionally, it enables accurate control over class balances in generated data.

In this study, we determined the total chromatic numbers along with their equitable and
neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Although previously observed in group-III compounds, remote epitaxy was until now limited to using the underlying SiO2 template for strain accommodation. Here, we demonstrate the growth of a Heusler compound, Cu2MnAl, on boron-passivated suspended graphene without such template support. Specifically, we show that the presence of Heusler layers leads to the emergence of a long-range, high-resistivity state in graphene, indicating the distortion of graphene's symmetry due to a charge imbalance. This phenomenon serves as a fingerprint for remote epitaxy, presenting a new method to detect and characterize such processes. Based on DFT calculations, we identify two distinct growth pathways for Cu2MnAl, with a total energy barrier of 0.35 eV/atom, and indicate that the resulting strain is partially offset by a 4.5% lattice expansion/contraction in the Heusler layers.

A code is referred to as $ \mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear if it results from projecting a specific type of code, which is an $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive code and has symmetry with respect to its constituent elements. In this study, a novel approach has been devised to effectively determine whether an $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-additive code qualifies as an $ \mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear code. Additionally, this research provides a comprehensive analysis of all $\mathbb{Z}_3\mathbb{Z}_9$-linear codes with a specific property, and determines their associated dual properties.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked with only a single relevant label, and thus is commonly encountered in real-life scenarios.  A potential solution to this challenge is a novel technique called virtual label propagation, in which the slow evolution of features in GAN models is leveraged to propagate each data feature to its corresponding class without requiring additional multi-class datasets.  Our method introduces a novel propagation network with a diagonal propagation matrix that can be efficiently optimized through an innovative objective function, allowing it to capture the relationship between class labels and data features, and thereby allows each class label to control its corresponding positive data feature.  Despite introducing some degree of noise, our method significantly outperforms the baseline V-AE method and is found to produce high-fidelity and multi-mode samples through the introduction of a noise regularization approach.  Our technique is further found to be effective in producing high-quality samples with improved class diversity and accuracy, and is robust to various types of generation tasks.  Source code is available at https://github.com/zhengqian9999999/Conditional-GAN-with-Single-Positive-Dataset.

This study investigates the property of energy dissipation associated with the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, introducing an upper bound that decreases over time, aligning with the natural energy loss observed in viscoelastic materials. The modified energy upper limit is related to the traditional energy function, with a scaling factor that varies from 1 to $1/2$ as time progresses, reflecting the alpha parameter's influence. A lower bound is also defined by the natural energy function, leading to an equivalent variation of the modified energy. Furthermore, the research extends to the phase-field model with two competing terms, specifically focusing on the sum of the time-fractional and classical local derivatives, and proves the well-posedness and long-term stability of the model's solution. The $L^2$ norm of the solution's derivative decays at a rate of $1/t^{1-\alpha}$, and the modified energy exhibits the same diversity as the classic model's energy, confirming the $ \alpha $-dependent $ 1/\Gamma(\alpha) $ factor's influence. These findings are derived without employing any Viscoelastic type assumptions, addressing the endogeneity problem of the model. The research also discusses the potential application of the time-fractional phase-field model to describe the deformation process of the mixture of viscoelastic substances.

The GNS construction forms a bridge between an abstract collection of physical observables in a C*-algebra and a specific state, representing a particular physical scenario. Notably, this process is not reversible for fixed algebras, as multiple distinct GNS representations can arise from a single irreducible scenario. However, the construction does allow for an inverse approach, where all possible outcomes from all states can be derived systematically. This paper aims to provide the detailed steps for this inverse approach.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that is a moderate fraction of the Einstein limit, while also matching observed X-rays and radio emissions.  Furthermore, the model predicts that the particle accelerators in these black hole disk environments create a power-law distribution with an acceleration rate of 2.2 to 2.5, with the exception of a particular instance where it occurs at a rate above the Einstein limit and has a more intense, twisted magnetic field, resulting in a different gamma-ray emission pattern.  This approach also explains gamma-ray data from observations by the Fermi-LAT, H.E. ESS, and the MAGIC collaborations, suggesting that magnetic reconnection in MAD state black hole disk systems can provide a comprehensive explanation for gamma-rays, X-rays, and radio emissions from these supermassive black hole systems.

This study develops a method to create smooth histograms and cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) for a set of portfolio returns, which can be used in a mean-CVaR framework for optimizing portfolios with concave utility functions. The method defines estimates of smooth histograms and CDFs based on the joint characteristics of individual asset returns and establishes an estimate of portfolio return as the sum of individual component returns. Consequently, this mean-CVaR estimation problem is formulated as an optimization problem with cumulative distribution-based constraints and is proven to have a finite number of local minima. The study also develops an efficient algorithm to find the optimal solution, and it is demonstrated through simulation that the proposed method and algorithm yield smoother efficient frontiers and more diverse portfolio selections compared to the traditional method using standard smooth techniques.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods are essential for this purpose. Listening to the heart by auscultation is a simple yet complex practice that requires comprehensive data for effective clinical application. This study introduces a novel approach to auscultation, utilizing intelligent sound analysis to identify and visualise abnormal heart sounds. Deep learning techniques are employed to analyze recorded heart sounds and determine the presence of murmurs or other abnormal sounds. A support vector machine classifies these sounds as either normal or abnormal based on the murmur detection results. Furthermore, a method using principal component analysis and heat maps is incorporated to visually represent the features contributing to the classification decision. This approach ensures accuracy in clinical decision-making while maintaining transparency in the process. Test data from multiple hospitals confirmed the effectiveness of this approach in comparing recorded heart sounds to a large database. This approach determines the presence of abnormalities, such as murmurs or other abnormal sounds, by classifying heart sounds as normal or abnormal based on support vector machine analysis following deep learning auscultation.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and fitness trackers allows users to easily access health data. This access encourages users to engage with their data, but also creates security threats from malicious actors who could exploit this connectivity to steal private information. To address this paradox, researchers need to tackle two key challenges: efficiently collecting data from multiple sources while preserving privacy, and personalizing data presentation to users' needs. Existing studies on using wearable technology for health purposes mostly focus on one aspect, either data collection or data presentation. This work aims to comprehensively review the literature, exploring the use of wearable technology for health purposes, data collection, data personalization, and the intersection of these fields. A unique contribution of this study lies in its in-depth analysis data personalization techniques for users who already have access to their own data. A distinctive feature of this study is its emphasis on the aggregation and personalization of wearable data from the user's perspective, a perspective that existing studies have mostly overlooked.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms, mathematical frameworks, and implementation approaches. Key research models, such as Janket's (2014) paradigm-shifting paradigm, are reviewed, and their comparative merits and limitations are examined through a detailed examination.

In string compactifications, we suggest that dark energy marks the universe's end, 
potentially triggered by decompactification, addressing the cosmological coincidence issue. 
Lack of stable de Sitter vacua forces us to model dark energy as a slow-rolling quintessence field. 
This process inevitably leads to a chaotic, universe-altering phase shift, likely after several hundred 
cosmological time cycles. Dark energy dominance, therefore, cannot persist forever, and the chance 
exists that we reside in the universe's first epoch. Our quintessence model illustrates the 
dysfunctional universe dynamics resulting from the descent of heavy states, when a multitude of particles 
are produced, overshadowing the quintessence's power. Additionally, our theory raises implications 
for the universe's early inflationary periods.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a complex issue. Research has already established parallels between these problems and well-known mathematical models. This study focuses on developing an optimal process plan for interviewing applicants by adapting a time-table scheduling problem. We adapt the Disjunctive Timeline Problem model, presenting a solution framework combining local search and reinforcement learning. This method allows us to test its performance against problem variations. Our results indicate that our approach outperforms existing solutions, providing a efficient process plan for applicants' interviewing.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17].

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into Monte Carlo simulations for Monte Carlo simulations, incorporating the leptoquark group's influence on the asymmetry of momentum in the created leptoquarks.

Temporal sequence analysis is a key challenge in many real-world applications, particularly when the sequence length is significant. Traditionally, deep learning methods address this challenge by leveraging recurrent neural networks or attention mechanisms. However, these methods often demand substantial training data and computational resources. In contrast, our proposed approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time (SGTM-TT), leverages Self-Organizing Maps and unsupervised learning techniques to achieve accurate one-step ahead predictions with minimal training data and computational cost. Notably, SGTM-TT preserves the temporal sequence structure while maintaining interpretability, a rarity among deep learning approaches. Experimental evaluations on seven real-world time series datasets reveal that our method ranks second overall and first among unsupervised and attention-based methods, demonstrating superior performance in prediction accuracy while outperforming traditional baseline models like ARIMA.

Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line intensities to be highly sensitive to molecular gas temperature. These lines therefore offer a direct and non-invasive way to estimate gas temperatures. We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector bosons at an energy scale of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier, around $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ or above, a problem arises, as we then encounter difficulty in resolving the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly consistently with the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing constraints. However, the proposed framework is compatible with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold for each flavor anomaly, with the parameter space for these anomalies overlapping in the energy range of $0.8\text{--}1.2\,\mathrm{TeV}$. Furthermore, we identify two primary methods to test this model at upcoming flavor and LHC experiments, namely through flavor-changing neutral current processes and through direct searches in dijet+dilepton final modes at the Large Hadron Collider.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of 5, or with a distance of 7, or with a
maximum possible overlap of 8 for a distance of 6.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that didn't match.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional approaches that treat each claim as independent, these datasets should represent the intricate web of dependencies between claims, which is essential for capturing the reasoning required to answer questions based on different parts of a document. To address this gap, our research presents a set of 5,049 pairs of questions and support excerpts taken from 800 papers in various domains. These papers were carefully selected through the active participation of various stakeholders, resulting in a diverse set of domains. Furthermore, each question is annotated with the part of the document that supports the answer, and is accompanied by an annotation of the relationship between the support and the question, as well as an indication of the other sections of the document that typically reference the support. Additionally, we developed automated metrics to evaluate the reliability of existing Answering systems, and our results show that current models struggle to accurately answer the diverse set of questions presented in our dataset.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential.

Acronyms serve as abbreviations that are prevalent in various texts, but their brevity can pose difficulties when interpreted, especially for individuals with reading disabilities. To address this issue, we are developing systems to interpret acronyms, starting with a neural network that translates acronyms to full terms in a specific domain. Building on this, our ultimate goal is to develop a translation model capable of handling plain language texts that have been replaced with acronyms.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In this process, molecules end up in a specific single quantum state. By leveraging the unique properties of these quasi-dark states, we demonstrate an atom-molecule conversion method where both spin-exchange and photoassociation collisional strengths influence the behavior of this system.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage compartment that we call a "box." Each box contains one or more data objects and is indexed by a unique pair of primer sites. We have devised a practical implementation of this architecture, allowing for flexible inner organization of objects within each box, and demonstrated its effectiveness with over 5 terabytes of diverse data. Our method enables efficient execution of common operations such as large-scale reads, targeted data retrievals, mass data deletions, and targeted data modifications with flexibility and economy, facilitating flexible data updates by enabling individual objects to be modified without affecting other objects that may share the same index. We have identified and addressed potential issues with our architecture, and suggested mitigation strategies.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines.

A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  A particular subtype called glioblastoma multiforme is especially malignant and accounts for 50-70% of all brain tumors.  Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has the highest diagnostic and detection rate for brain tumors.  This study employs a deep learning algorithm, a modified UNet 25D model, to automatically identify and segment MR images.  To do so, it analyzed 155 multi-channel three-dimensional MRI images from the Automatic Multi-Modality Medical Image Segmentation (AMASS) dataset.  The model's accuracy in classifying images was 99.4%, while its performance in segmenting images was assessed using various metrics such as Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Hausdorff Distance (HD), and overlap rate.  The obtained results indicate that our proposed framework is a viable and effective solution for identifying, classifying, and segmenting brain tumors.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from being practical for optimization. To address these issues, we introduce an efficient volume-based DRCO model that utilizes a hierarchical coarse-fine architecture to achieve precise shadow simulation while maintaining high computational efficiency. By utilizing a single network for volume texture prediction, we utilize the differentiable nature of rasterization to utilize the shadow coherence across multiple optimization views, eliminating the need for additional network components. Our initial experiments demonstrate that our differentiable renderer outperforms the benchmarks in terms of overall quality and shadow accuracy.

A popular technique, widely used in video technology for over five decades, is interlacing, which halves the resolution by displaying only half the scan lines at any given moment, with the remaining lines presented in the next frame. This technique enhances bandwidth efficiency but results in reduced image quality. With the advent of modern high-definition displays capable of presenting complete images at each moment, there's now greater demand for enhanced video quality. To meet this need, super-resolution techniques have been developed to enhance interlaced videos. Due to their widespread prevalence, particularly in sports broadcasts, there's even more urgency to upgrade standard-definition videos, often delivered in an interlaced format, to high-definition formats. Such upgrades require both deinterlacing and super-resolution techniques. This paper presents a deep learning-based method that accomplishes both deinterlacing and upscaling standard-definition (720p) videos to high-definition (1080p) resolution. Our proposed end-to-end deep neural network processess a pair of overlapped interlaced video frames and produces a single high-definition frame in real-time. This method demonstrates superior performance to state-of-the-art methods in both deinterlacing and super-resolution tasks, with up to a 25% improvement in Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR).

The investigation revealed a disparity of approximately 0.1 fm in the root mean square radius of the neutron point distribution between non-relativistic mean field models and their relativistic counterparts. Further analysis revealed the discrepancy arises due to varying product values of the effective mass and one-body potential strength within the respective frameworks, with those values being governed by the Hugenholtz-Van Hove theorem. In contrast, the thickness of the neutron skin was found not to solely correlate with the symmetry potential but rather was heavily dependent on the nucleon effective mass.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating the results with open-source bathymetry and flow velocity data from the Rhine river.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, benefiting future research in machine learning.

This research uses a control problem in catalytic fixed bed reactors to apply theories from microdifferential equations and adaptive boundary control. The goal is to achieve an optimal temperature distribution within the reactor by adjusting the temperature at the inlet. A significant challenge in this field is the lack of observability for the full Neumann problem due to the parabolic nature of the associated PDE. To address this issue, an infinite depth approximation is employed, transforming the model into a system of two coupled heat equations with a unique point of non-control. Despite this obstacle, a solution is found through an adaptive boundary control strategy, using only boundary temperature and gradient controls on a finite section of the reactor.

This note presents a new category of map functions, specifically tangent map functions from Euclidean space to Euclidean space, which is a more specialized variant of the map functions studied in the study of colored broken submersions. It defines a new, more specialized type of map function, which is a variant of the map functions studied in the b-principle. It also demonstrates that the map functions from Euclidean space to Euclidean space, which are in the map functions from Euclidean space to Euclidean space, which are not strictly Euclidean submersions, can be homotopically connected within the map functions from Euclidean space to Euclidean space, which are in the map functions from Euclidean space to Euclidean space, which are not strictly Euclidean submersions, based on the dimension of the target Euclidean space, specifically when the target Euclidean space has an odd dimension greater than one. It extends the previous proof in the paper of oriented colored broken submersions, which was a variant of the map functions from Euclidean space to Euclidean space, which are not strictly Euclidean submersions, based on the dimension of the target Euclidean space, specifically when the target Euclidean space has an odd dimension greater than one.
